title: Here's How These 6 Big Bank Stocks Make Their Money
detail:
Here's How These 6 Big Bank Stocks Make Their Money
Patrick Sanders, The Motley Fool

JPM

JPMorgan Chase (NYSE: JPM), Bank of America (NYSE: BAC), Wells Fargo (NYSE: WFC), Citigroup (NYSE: C), Goldman Sachs (NYSE: GS), and Morgan Stanley (NYSE: MS) have something in common: They're among the biggest names in American banking. But how they make their money can be surprisingly different.

Some rely heavily on traditional lending, collecting interest on mortgages, credit cards, and business loans. Others generate billions from investment banking, trading, and managing money for wealthy clients. Some do a little bit of everything.

Missed Nvidia in 2009? This Rare Signal Is Flashing Again. In 2009, a "Double Down" signal flashed for a little-known chipmaker called Nvidia. For the first time in years, that same "Total Conviction" signal is flashing for a company 1/100th the size of Nvidia. Continue »

All six banks reported third-quarter earnings on Oct. 13 and 14, giving investors a closer look at the businesses driving their profits. Here's what stood out with these six bank stocks.

Image source: Getty Images.
JPMorgan Chase: A little bit of everything

JPMorgan Chase is the U.S.'s largest bank, and one of its biggest advantages is its ability to earn money in multiple ways. Its asset management business generated $5.9 billion in fees during Q3, a 15% increase from a year ago. Investment banking fees climbed 13% to $3 billion, including a 32% jump in advisory fees.

Don't overlook the credit card business. Card income surged 25% to $1.43 billion, helped by higher annual fees. Meanwhile, revenue from Card Services & Auto increased 15% to $8.28 billion. Even automobile leasing is contributing to growth. Operating lease income reached $1.2 billion, up from $987 million a year earlier, as the bank expanded its portfolio of leased vehicles.

That's the appeal of JPMorgan Chase's business model. It can generate revenue from everyday consumer banking while collecting substantial fees from wealthy investors and corporate clients.

Bank of America: Wealth management is doing the heavy lifting

Bank of America is another banking giant with several revenue streams, but its wealth management business has become a particularly important source of growth. Global Wealth & Investment Management generated $7.1 billion in Q3 revenue, up 13%, while net income reached $1.54 billion. Asset management fees climbed to approximately $4.5 billion from $3.9 billion a year earlier. Client balances reached a whopping $5.1 trillion.

Bank of America also makes substantial money from a business that most people rarely think about. Its Global Transaction Services operation helps companies manage payments, cash, and other financial transactions. Revenue from that business increased 11% to $3.04 billion.

Investing.com -- Citi has identified Circle as its top pick in the regulated stablecoin and digital payment infrastructure sector, citing the company's position as a leading beneficiary of stablecoin adoption and modernization of global payment systems.

Circle's recent quarter demonstrated that its USDC stablecoin is transitioning from a stored-value product into a broader financial infrastructure layer, according to Citi analysts. While USDC circulation remained largely flat, transaction activity, mint and redeem volumes, payment flows, and Cross-Chain Transfer Protocol adoption all accelerated, suggesting network utility is expanding faster than balances.

Unsure what to buy ahead of earnings? Our AI's recent pre-earnings calls delivered gains of +77% to +118% after results dropped. See this month's earnings picks »

Circle (CRCL)

Citi maintains Circle as its top pick despite lowering fiscal 2027 estimates. The firm noted several positive developments, including accelerating Cross-Chain Transfer Protocol transaction processing volume with emerging network effects, record mint and redemption activity, and stronger-than-expected Arc platform launch with solid ecosystem adoption. The Cross-Chain Transfer Protocol monetization is underway, with meaningful revenue contribution targeted for 2027. Financial institution adoption is also broadening across payment, fintech, capital markets, and settlement applications. However, Citi acknowledged challenges including lower net reserve margins due to renewed Binance economics pressure in 2027, flat USDC circulation despite improving utility metrics, and an earnings beat driven primarily by Arc revenue recognition rather than core reserve economics.

The firm modestly increased fiscal 2027 circulation and reserve-income assumptions based on stronger network adoption and transaction activity, but reduced near-term reserve-margin expectations to reflect the full-quarter impact of renewed distribution agreements. Citi also materially reduced fiscal 2027 other revenue projections to $400 million from previous estimates after correcting a modeling error related to Arc revenue recognition, though this remains above the Visible Alpha Consensus of $320 million. Transaction and platform revenue remain minimal relative to reserve income, representing an ongoing investor consideration.

title: Forget pricey JPMorgan: Is this turnaround bank the better rebound bet?

Forget pricey JPMorgan: Is this turnaround bank the better rebound bet?

Investing.com — With Citigroup (NYSE:C) expecting the Federal Reserve to hold off on rate cuts until June 2027, investors are sorting banks by who can keep earning while rates stay high. JPMorgan Chase (NYSE:JPM) is the usual answer, at nearly 14 times earnings, and Bank of America (NYSE:BAC) has barely moved in a year.

Investors have been willing to pay for safety, but it's Citigroup that gained 29.6% over that stretch and still trades at 11.4 times earnings.

That lower multiple shows lingering doubt about a bank still in the middle of a restructuring, and a monthly data-driven screen can test it against each new set of results. ProPicks AI, InvestingPro's AI-driven stock-picking service, added Citigroup to its Beat the S&P 500 strategy for November. The bank shares that line-up with an online travel booking leader, a high-margin commercial biopharma company and a commercial jet-turbine maker.

See the full list of AI-picked holdings: Explore the Beat the S&P 500 strategy on InvestingPro

Cutting Costs While the Services Franchise Grows

Citigroup's latest quarter backed the turnaround plan with results. Earnings per share of $2.85 beat estimates by 7.5%, revenue rose 8% in the strongest third quarter for revenue in a decade, and return on tangible common equity (ROTCE) reached 11.5%, up 180 basis points from a year earlier. Management lifted its full-year ROTCE target to above 11%.

Most of that growth came from the units Citi is betting on. Services revenue grew 15% with a 31.2% ROTCE, Wealth revenue also rose 15% on $38 billion of net new investment assets, and equity capital markets revenue jumped 77%, helped by leading six of the largest equity deals of the quarter. Meanwhile the efficiency ratio improved to 58.5% from 64.7%, with more than $1 billion of severance booked this year and stranded costs trimmed to about a $100 million quarterly run rate.

Consumer cards remain the soft spot, with revenue flat as partner payments and rewards costs climb. Shares also fell 3.48% in premarket trading after the report, on caution over fourth-quarter markets seasonality and the pace of capital deployment.

Weighing the Discount Against the Returns Gap

Wall Street consensus estimates compiled on InvestingPro put 2027 earnings at $12.78 a share, which pushes the forward multiple below 10 times. InvestingPro data also show a PEG ratio of 0.26 for Citigroup, against 0.75 for Bank of America. Tangible book value per share rose 6% to $101.59, which puts the stock at about 1.2 times tangible book. Management has repurchased $13.3 billion of stock so far this year, more than all of 2025, and has raised its dividend for four straight years. The median analyst price target is $150.71, though earnings revisions over the past 90 days lean negative.

Investing.com -- Citi cut its rating for BJ's Wholesale Club (NYSE: BJ) to Neutral from Buy on Friday, citing a more balanced risk/reward after the stock's strong run.

The bank nudged its price target up to $113 from $111.

Citi expects BJ's third-quarter same-store sales to beat both the company's plan of 2% to 3% and the Street's 2.8% estimate. Warehouse clubs are seeing strong traffic as high gas prices draw shoppers, and investors have flocked to staples retailers as an inflation hedge.

However, Citi said "there's a lot of optimism priced into shares at this point," with the stock trading at about 22 times its fiscal 2027 EPS estimate, above its five-year average of about 19 times.

"We are also concerned that some of the sales strength in the near-term is driven by one-time promotional events, tariff refunds and litigation settlement that will be difficult to lap next year," the bank wrote.

Citi also flagged rising competition among warehouse clubs to grow memberships, particularly as Walmart's combined Walmart+ and Sam's Club Plus offering scales.

The bank said the main risk to its downgrade would be stronger-than-expected third-quarter sales and EPS.

In the same note, Citi previewed earnings across retail. It expects beat-and-raise quarters from Ulta Beauty, Best Buy, Williams-Sonoma and Ollie's Bargain Outlet. Among home improvement retailers, it sees Home Depot's same-store sales outperforming Lowe's, and it views both as stocks to lean into if rates decline.

title: JPM Flags Higher Rate Risks: Can Its Balance Sheet Stay Resilient?
detail:
JPM Flags Higher Rate Risks: Can Its Balance Sheet Stay Resilient?
Swayta Shah
Fri, November 6, 2026 at 7:12 AM CST 3 min read
JPM
BAC
C
Explore stocks on Coinbase
Trading disclosure

JPMorgan JPM remains focused on maintaining balance sheet resilience amid expectations of structurally higher interest rates. At the Nov. 5 BancAnalysts Association of Boston Conference, Charles Bristow, head of Treasury and chief investment officer, emphasized disciplined duration management, stable operating deposits and rigorous stress testing to navigate interest rate volatility.

Bristow noted that JPMorgan has historically avoided excessive exposure to longer-duration securities, helping limit valuation risks as interest rates increased. Its emphasis on operating deposits linked to payments, custody and checking activities also supports funding stability, although unusually sharp rate increases could pressure deposit costs.

The company's underlying performance reinforces this resilience. During the first nine months of 2026, reported net interest income (NII) increased 11% year over year to $77.9 billion. NII excluding Markets rose 4% to $71.7 billion, supported by deposit and loan growth. JPMorgan expects fourth-quarter 2026 NII of approximately $28 billion, implying full-year NII of $106.2 billion, while NII excluding Markets is projected to be $97.2 billion. Its preliminary 2027 outlook projects NII excluding Markets of nearly $107 billion, reflecting almost 10% growth backed by balance sheet expansion and higher rates.

However, Bristow cautioned that proposed regulatory capital requirements could undermine returns from certain low-risk intermediation activities. Rapid interest rate repricing and tighter systemwide liquidity also pose risks.

Overall, JPMorgan's diversified franchise, disciplined asset-liability management and stable deposit base support its earnings outlook. Nevertheless, regulatory uncertainty, funding costs and interest rate volatility warrant monitoring, suggesting a balanced investment approach.

How are JPM's Peers Expected to Fare in a Higher-Rate Regime?

Two close peers of JPMorgan are Bank of America BAC and Citigroup C.

Bank of America is well-positioned to benefit from higher interest rates, supported by its asset-sensitive balance sheet, fixed-rate asset repricing and loan growth. Bank of America expects 2026 NII to increase approximately 8% year over year. However, higher deposit costs could partly offset these benefits.

Citigroup is positioned to benefit from higher interest rates, given its asset-sensitive balance sheet, loan growth and investment portfolio repricing. Citigroup expects 2026 NII, excluding Markets, to increase in the mid-to-high 6% range year over year. However, rising deposit costs could partly offset these benefits.

Adobe Is Down 29% This Year. Time to Sell or Buy More? ©@Donatello Trisolino from Pexels via Canva, @inkdrop via Canva
Key Takeaways

Adobe stock is down 29% in 2026, and on Nov. 4 Citi cut it to Sell with a $207 target, expecting a weaker fiscal 2027 outlook.

The business is still growing: third-quarter revenue rose 13%, and analysts expect normalized EPS to climb from $20.94 in fiscal 2025 to $31.20 in fiscal 2028.

The stock trades far below its five-year average forward P/E, and Adobe's free cash flow lets it buy back a meaningful slice of its shares each year.

At this price, a lot of bad news is already priced in, which makes Adobe a stock to buy more of ahead of its expected Dec. 9 report.

Adobe (ADBE:NASDAQ) is down 29% in 2026, and Wall Street keeps piling on. On Nov. 4, Citi cut the stock to Sell and lowered its price target to $207 from $250.

Citi is the latest in a string of downgrades this fall. Goldman Sachs repeated its Sell with a $200 target on Oct. 2, Wells Fargo cut Adobe two notches to Underweight with a $225 target on Oct. 12, and HSBC moved to Hold at $267 a day later.

But the selling looks overdone.

TIKR tracks 39 analysts on Adobe. How many say "Buy"?

See the full breakdown of Buy, Hold, and Sell ratings on Adobe, along with Wall Street's revenue and earnings estimates, all in one place. More than 500,000 investors use TIKR to research stocks like this one. See Adobe's Analyst Ratings

Citi is bracing for a weaker 2027

Citi analyst Tyler Radke expects Adobe to give a weaker fiscal 2027 forecast when it reports fourth-quarter results. He cut his net new annual recurring revenue estimates to $1.5 billion for fiscal 2027, down $470 million, and to $1.45 billion for fiscal 2028, down $500 million.

Some of the worry is about who will give that forecast. Shantanu Narayen hands the CEO job to Anil Chakravarthy on Dec. 1 and becomes executive chair. David Wadhwani, who ran Adobe's creativity and productivity business, is leaving, and Steve Day is serving as interim CFO.

The bigger worry is AI, and whether new tools will undercut what Adobe can charge for its software. On the Nov. 2 episode of The Prof G Pod, Scott Galloway asked whether AI is killing software, and said that so far the market has decided "the rumors of SaaS's death have been greatly exaggerated."

Adobe shareholders might disagree. But Galloway also pointed out that Adobe was one of 32 software partners when OpenAI launched its new marketplace. That's not how you treat a company you're about to replace.

So far, the business is fine

In its fiscal third quarter, which ended Aug. 28, Adobe's revenue grew 13% to a record $6.76 billion, and its total annualized recurring revenue rose 11.2% to $27.50 billion. Non-GAAP EPS climbed 15% to $6.13, and management raised its full-year non-GAAP EPS target to $24.45-$24.50.
